To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified two new subtypes of mouse On-Off direction selective retinal ganglion cell (DSGC), which are distinguished by the expression of dopamine receptor 4 and thyrotropine releasing hormone receptor (DRD4 and TRHR, respectively).

1) there are two genetically identified populations in the mouse retina that respond strongly to a stimulus moving posteriorly and weakly to a stimulus moving in the opposite direction, 2) these two populations can be distinguished by their physiological and anatomical features, 3) both populations project to the dorsal lateral...

there are at least two genetically identified populations, TRHR- and DRD4-ON-OFF DSGCs, that are directionally tuned to motion in the same direction but that have different directional tuning, different projection patterns to different parts of the brain, different responses to light flashes, and different responses to light flickers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural circuit mechanisms of visual perception.
how information is transmitted through the retina to the brain, and how the brain processes this information.
the visual system of the mouse and the retina in particular.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the retina of the mouse is more complex than previously thought and that it contains a larger variety of direction selective retinal ganglion cell subtypes than previously known.
there is a great diversity of direction-selective retino-geniculo-colliculo-thalamo-recipient neurons that process and transmit visual information.

the retina contains a diverse population of On-Off direction selective retinal ganglion cell subtypes that are not only differentially distributed in the brain, but also differentially tuned to the visual stimulus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a new type of On-Off directionally selective retinal ganglion cell (DSGC) that projects to an uncharacterized thalamic nucleus, the zona incerta.
the retina contains more than four subtypes of DSGCs, and they have different brain projections.
there is a greater diversity in On-Off DSCG than was previously appreciated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are at least two distinct populations of On- and Off-direction-selective retinal neurons that project to different brain areas and that process visual motion in different ways.
there is a greater diversity in direction selectivity in the retina than previously appreciated, and this diversity is reflected in the brain areas that receive information from these cells.
On-Off DSCGs are more diverse than previously thought and that the brain contains more structures than previously known that receive visual information about the direction of motion.
